For instance, palladium-
catalyzed bisfunctional cyclization (e.g., silastannylation,
distannylation, and germastannylation),<sup>8</sup> borylation carbocyc-
lization,<sup>9</sup> and multicomponent cascade carbocyclization of
bisallenes<sup>10</sup> have been reported.<sup>11</sup> Furthermore, the transition
metal-catalyzed carbocyclization/arylation of bisallenes has
also been gradually implemented (Scheme 1a).<sup>12−14</sup> In 2009,
Ma and co-workers reported a palladium-catalyzed regiose-
lective cascade carbocyclization of 1,5-bisallenes with prop-
argylic carbonates and arylboronic acids, ofering an eficient
route to bicyclo[4.3.0]nonenes.<sup>12</sup> Subsequently, Backvall ̈ and
Volla realized a palladium-catalyzed carbocyclization/arylation
of 1,4-bisallenes for preparing six-membered carbocycles.
More recently, our group achieved the first earth-abundant
cobalt- catalyzed regio- and diastereoselective carbocycliza-
tion/arylation of 1,5-bisallenes, yielding cis-disubstituted
pyrrole derivatives.<sup>14</sup> Despite the aforementioned advances,
the investigation of carbocyclization/alkenylation of bisallenes
with alkenylboronic acids is limited, and new methods for
constructing diferent cyclic skeletons are also in high
demand.<sup>12−14</sup>

carbocyclization/alkenylation of bisallenes and alkenylboronic
acids (Scheme 1b). This catalytic system accommodates not
only carbon-, nitrogen-, and oxygen-linked bisallenes but also
alkenyl and arylboronic acids, producing bicyclo[3.2.0]-
heptanes under mild conditions with high selectivity.

Based on our comprehensive mechanistic studies (for
details, see Scheme S1) and previous works,<sup>6,17,18</sup> the possible
reaction mechanism of this nickel-catalyzed cascade carbocyc-
lization/alkenylation of bisallenes and alkenylboronic acids is
shown in Scheme 3. Initially, 1a undergoes regioselective
oxidative cyclometalation with nickel(0)/dppf to yield five-
membered nickelacycle A. Next, the reductive elimination of
complex A forms 3aa′, while regenerating the nickel catalyst.
Notably, the nickel-catalyzed [2 + 2] cycloaddition of bisallene
1a is a fast process, and it would not be obstructed by the
addition of 2a. After the complete conversion of 1a, the
nickel(0) species proceeds to initiate a second catalytic cycle.
The oxidative addition of nickel(0) species with MeOH
produces nickel hydride complex B. Then, coordination and
regioselective migratory insertion of 3aa′ with nickel hydride
complex B result in the formation of allylic nickel complex C.
The transition state for this process shows that nickel hydride
insertion from the front side encounters more steric hindrance
than that from the back side. Subsequently, complex C
undergoes transmetalation with 2a to yield complex D. Finally,
complex D undergoes reductive elimination to aford 3aa and
regenerate the nickel(0) species. The overall reaction
mechanism contains two catalytic cycles. The first is the
nickel-catalyzed regioselective [2 + 2] cycloaddition of
bisallenes, and the second involves the subsequent hydro-
alkenylation of the diene intermediate with alkenylboronic
acids. This represents a unique cascade process for the
transition metal-catalyzed carbocyclization/alkenylation of
bisallenes.<sup>12−14</sup>
To demonstrate the synthetic utility of this method, we first
performed late-stage modification of a drug molecule (Scheme
4a). When celecoxib-derived bisallene 5 was subjected to the
standard conditions, cascade carbocyclization/alkenylation
product 6 was successfully obtained in good yield. Signifi-
cantly, the reaction between 1a and 2a could be scaled up to
the subgram level, yielding 3aa with sustained eficiency
(Scheme 4b). Furthermore, downstream transformations of
3aa were conducted (Scheme 4c). Under a hydrogen
atmosphere, the 1,1- and 1,2-disubstituted alkenes in 3aa
could be readily reduced to form bicyclo[3.2.0]heptane 7 in
quantitative yield with excellent diastereoselectivity. Addition-
ally, in the presence of an iridium catalyst, one-pot hydro-
boration/oxidation selectively occurred at the 1,1-disubstituted
alkene of 3aa, although with relatively low diastereoselectivity.
In conclusion, we achieved the first nickel-catalyzed cascade
carbocyclization/alkenylation of bisallenes and organoboronic
acids. Carbon-, nitrogen-, and oxygen-linked bisallenes and
alkenyl and arylboronic acids are well tolerated in this reaction,
resulting in the formation of various bicyclo[3.2.0]heptane
derivatives with high selectivity and eficiency. Mechanistic
experiments indicate that this reaction occurs through a unique
two-step cascade process. It starts with a nickel-catalyzed [2 +
2] cycloaddition of bisallenes, followed by a nickel-catalyzed
regioselective hydroalkenylation of the diene intermediate with
alkenylboronic acids. Moreover, the practical utility of this
method is showcased through the late-stage modification of
drug molecules, scale-up experiments, and downstream
transformations. Further investigations of the nickel-catalyzed
carbocyclization of bisallenes are ongoing in our laboratory and
will be reported in the near future.

Based on our comprehensive mechanistic studies (for
details, see Scheme S1) and previous works,<sup>6,17,18</sup> the possible
reaction mechanism of this nickel-catalyzed cascade carbocyc-
lization/alkenylation of bisallenes and alkenylboronic acids is
shown in Scheme 3. Initially, 1a undergoes regioselective
oxidative cyclometalation with nickel(0)/dppf to yield five-
membered nickelacycle A. Next, the reductive elimination of
complex A forms 3aa′, while regenerating the nickel catalyst.
Notably, the nickel-catalyzed [2 + 2] cycloaddition of bisallene
1a is a fast process, and it would not be obstructed by the
addition of 2a. After the complete conversion of 1a, the
nickel(0) species proceeds to initiate a second catalytic cycle.
The oxidative addition of nickel(0) species with MeOH
produces nickel hydride complex B. Then, coordination and
regioselective migratory insertion of 3aa′ with nickel hydride
complex B result in the formation of allylic nickel complex C.
The transition state for this process shows that nickel hydride
insertion from the front side encounters more steric hindrance
than that from the back side. Subsequently, complex C
undergoes transmetalation with 2a to yield complex D. Finally,
complex D undergoes reductive elimination to aford 3aa and
regenerate the nickel(0) species. The overall reaction
mechanism contains two catalytic cycles. The first is the
nickel-catalyzed regioselective [2 + 2] cycloaddition of
bisallenes, and the second involves the subsequent hydro-
alkenylation of the diene intermediate with alkenylboronic
acids. This represents a unique cascade process for the
transition metal-catalyzed carbocyclization/alkenylation of
bisallenes.<sup>12−14</sup>
To demonstrate the synthetic utility of this method, we first
performed late-stage modification of a drug molecule (Scheme
4a). When celecoxib-derived bisallene 5 was subjected to the
standard conditions, cascade carbocyclization/alkenylation
product 6 was successfully obtained in good yield. Signifi-
cantly, the reaction between 1a and 2a could be scaled up to
the subgram level, yielding 3aa with sustained eficiency
(Scheme 4b). Furthermore, downstream transformations of
3aa were conducted (Scheme 4c). Under a hydrogen
atmosphere, the 1,1- and 1,2-disubstituted alkenes in 3aa
could be readily reduced to form bicyclo[3.2.0]heptane 7 in
quantitative yield with excellent diastereoselectivity. Addition-
ally, in the presence of an iridium catalyst, one-pot hydro-
boration/oxidation selectively occurred at the 1,1-disubstituted
alkene of 3aa, although with relatively low diastereoselectivity.
In conclusion, we achieved the first nickel-catalyzed cascade
carbocyclization/alkenylation of bisallenes and organoboronic
acids. Carbon-, nitrogen-, and oxygen-linked bisallenes and
alkenyl and arylboronic acids are well tolerated in this reaction,
resulting in the formation of various bicyclo[3.2.0]heptane
derivatives with high selectivity and eficiency. Mechanistic
experiments indicate that this reaction occurs through a unique
two-step cascade process. It starts with a nickel-catalyzed [2 +
2] cycloaddition of bisallenes, followed by a nickel-catalyzed
regioselective hydroalkenylation of the diene intermediate with
alkenylboronic acids. Moreover, the practical utility of this
method is showcased through the late-stage modification of
drug molecules, scale-up experiments, and downstream
transformations. Further investigations of the nickel-catalyzed
carbocyclization of bisallenes are ongoing in our laboratory and
will be reported in the near future.
